newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech central bank head says wage hope unrealistic.
newsitem.headline: Czech central bank head says wage hope unrealistic.

text.p: Czech National Bank governor Josef Tosovsky, in a thinly veiled attack on Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, said on Monday that politicians had made implementing austerity measures more difficult by raising wage hopes unrealistically.

Although Tosovsky did not mention the prime minister by name, he referred to politicians' remarks before the 1996 elections that the Czech standard of living could quickly rise to the European Union (EU) average.
Klaus caused a storm before the last election by promising that wages, which in purchasing power terms are around half the EU average, could double by the year 2000.
"Due to higher expectations, it is now more difficult to implement tough measures than if politicians had not been so optimistic," Tosovsky told the Financial Times World Gold Conference here.

Due to a sharp economic slowdown, a depreciation of the Czech crown and a drop in tax revenues, the government has pledged to take drastic measures to cut public expenditure and in particular, slam the brakes on wage growth.
Nominal industrial wages jumped 14.7 percent in April while industrial output this year has slowed sharply, and the government expects almost no economic growth in the first quarter.
The central bank has consistently warned that wage growth poses a threat to its efforts to keep inflation down. May inflation was 6.3 percent year-on-year.
Tosovsky repeated that last summer's sharp monetary squeeze, which was tightened further to protect the crown, had been partly a response to the sharp growth in wages.
The discount rate was raised to 13 percent from 10.5 on May 27.
